# Storage in laravel says symlink - no such file or directory

You are attempting to create a symbolic link from your application's `storage` directory, located within `public_html/app`, to an external location at `/../../files`. The error message `symlink(): No such file or directory` is straightforward: the PHP runtime cannot find the target path you specified. This usually happens when relative path resolution fails on shared hosting environments where the document root and application structure differ from your local development setup.

On localhost, your command likely works because your working directory matches the expected location of the `files` folder. However, in a shared hosting environment, the URL path `/../../files` does not necessarily translate to the physical file system path you expect. Relative paths are resolved against the current working directory and the document root, which often causes confusion when deploying Laravel on platforms that serve files from `public_html`.

To resolve this, you must ensure the target directory exists before attempting to create the symlink. Use the following command to manually create the directory if it is missing:

```bash
mkdir -p /../../files
```

Once the directory exists, run the storage link command again from within your application's root (or specify the source and destination explicitly). Note that you should execute this from the `public_html/app` directory or ensure the script resolves paths correctly relative to the document root. If you are on a shared host, you might not have permission to create symlinks outside the `public_html` directory. In such cases, consider moving your `files` directory inside `public_html` (e.g., `public_html/files`) and linking it locally:

```bash
cd /path/to/public_html/app
php artisan storage:link
```

This approach avoids cross-directory symlink issues and keeps all assets within the allowed document root.

If you cannot move the files due to constraints, check whether your hosting provider allows symbolic links at all. Some shared hosts disable `symlink()` for security reasons or require links to stay within the same domain. If symlinks are blocked, you may need to configure Laravel to write directly to a writable directory instead of using a symlink.

Laravel expects the `storage` symlink to point to a physical directory where uploaded files reside. Ensure that the target directory has proper permissions (typically 755 or 775) and is owned by the same user running PHP. Misconfigured permissions can also lead to write failures even if the symlink exists.

In some hosting environments, you may need to use an absolute path instead of a relative one when configuring `APP_STORAGE_PATH` in your `.env` file. For example:

```env
APP_STORAGE_PATH=/path/to/public_html/files
```

Be cautious when modifying this value; Laravel will attempt to create the symlink automatically on subsequent migrations or cache clears only if the target directory exists and is valid.

If you continue to face issues, verify whether your `.htaccess` file or server configuration (e.g., `nginx.conf`) blocks symlink execution. Some hosts replace symlinks with copies unless explicitly allowed. In those cases, consider uploading files directly via FTP or SFTP to the intended location rather than relying on the symlink mechanism.

For production deployments, always test your storage setup before going live. Use tools like `php artisan file:scan` (if available in your version) or manually check uploaded files to confirm accessibility. If you need further assistance with Laravel hosting configurations, refer to [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) for community-driven guidance on deployment best practices.
